tour.title: Baku: Old City to the Caspian
tour.summary: Eight centuries in under three kilometres of walking — walled khans' palaces, Silk Road caravanserais, a funicular ride, and sunset over the Caspian.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Baku — the City of Winds. And before you ask: yes, the wind is real, it has a name (the khazri blows from the north, the gilavar from the south), and by the end of this walk you will have opinions about both.

Here is the deal with this city. Two thousand years ago it was a walled town of fire-worshippers on a hill above an inland sea. Then the oil came — Baku drilled some of the world's first oil wells in the 1840s, and by 1900 half the world's oil came out of the ground around you. The Nobel brothers and the Rothschilds built mansions here. Penniless teachers became millionaires before lunch. They called it the Paris of the Caucasus, and they were only half joking.

That oil money built the Baku you see — the Flame Towers, the boulevards, the airport that looks like a spaceship. It also shapes the politics. Azerbaijan is rich, secular and Muslim-majority, and it has been run by one family since 1993 — first Heydar Aliyev, then his son Ilham. Supporters credit them with stability and staggering growth; critics call it a dynasty with no exit. Meanwhile the wound this country carries is Nagorno-Karabakh: Armenians and Azerbaijanis fought two wars over it, the second in 2020, and in 2023 Azerbaijan took it back in full while some 100,000 Armenians fled. You will stand at Martyrs' Alley, where that history is buried. Read the names. Both sides mourn; only one side's cemetery is on this walk.

Our walk follows that whole story in order. We start inside the medieval walls of Icherisheher, the Old City, with a mysterious tower nobody can explain, a palace built by a dynasty that ruled for eight hundred years, a Friday mosque, a Silk Road inn, and the world's most charming tiny museum. Then we leave the walls through the double gates, cross the café buzz of Fountain Square, and cheat the big hill the local way — riding the little Soviet funicular to the top. Up there: the best panorama in Azerbaijan and its most solemn memorial, side by side. We finish down on the Caspian promenade as the Flame Towers light up.

Practical things. Walked end to end this is about 5.2 kilometres and around eighty minutes on foot. The steep 1.8-kilometre climb up to Highland Park is the one stretch to ride, not hike — that is what the little Soviet funicular is for. Museum tickets are a few manat each and every price I quote is an educated guess — Azerbaijani prices move, so check at the gate and never blame the voice in your ear. Bring cash in manat for small tickets and tea. And one house rule: mosques close to visitors during the five daily prayers. A shut door is prayer time, not rejection. Go drink tea and come back.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Flat cobbled lanes in the Old City, the steep hill is ridden via funicular, then a gentle downhill walk to the boulevard. The Maiden Tower's internal stairs are steep and narrow; the Old City underfoot is cobbles and worn stone.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start early afternoon, around 1 to 2pm, so the museums are open and you reach the hilltop for late golden light. Time the viewpoint for the hour before sunset, and finish on the boulevard as the Flame Towers switch on their LED flames after dark. Mornings work too, but the light over the bay is an evening show.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Maiden Tower
stops.narration:
Look up. That is the Qız Qalası — the Maiden Tower — and it is the reason Baku has a skyline at all. Twenty-nine and a half metres of pale limestone, eight floors, walls five metres thick at the base, and not a single person on earth can tell you for certain why it was built.

That is not an exaggeration. The current tower went up in the 12th century, but its foundations are far older — some stones look Sasanian, some archaeologists whisper about Zoroastrian fire-temple roots going back twenty-five centuries. Theories for its purpose include: watchtower, observatory, lighthouse, fortress keep, and temple. It has a famous ribbed buttress jutting toward the sea that appears in no other tower of its kind, and every theory has to explain that fin and fails. Pick your favourite. The locals did: legend says a khan's daughter, ordered to marry against her will, asked to be given this tower first — then climbed to the top and threw herself into the sea rather than obey. Hence the name. Almost certainly untrue. Completely unforgettable.

Go inside, because the tower is a museum now, and the climb is the exhibition. Each of the eight levels covers a chapter — stone age, fire-worship, khans, oil barons — and the staircase gets narrower and older-feeling as you rise, which is either atmospheric or a health-and-safety seminar depending on your knees.

And then the roof. From up there you get the whole walk in one glance: the Old City's rooftops at your feet, the Flame Towers doing their glassy thing on the hill, and the grey-blue Caspian stretching out like a rumour. Eight centuries of Baku, visible without turning your head. Stand there a minute. Everything else today is footnotes to this view.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Museum ticket around 15 ₼, roughly. Prices move and foreign-visitor pricing can differ, so verify at the gate and carry small manat notes.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 10:00 to 18:00, sometimes longer in summer. Ticket office usually closes an hour before the tower. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: steep narrow stone stairs between all eight floors, low doorways, uneven steps. The plaza around the base is level cobbles.
stops.insiderTip: Climb slowly and look at the masonry as you go — you can see where the 12th-century builders joined older stonework. At the top, find the sea-facing fin: that strange rib is the tower's great unsolved mystery.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the tower plaza and walk about sixty metres north up the lane, into the small stone courtyard with the big carved portal. That is the Bukhara Caravanserai, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bukhara Caravanserai
stops.narration:
Step off the lane and into the 15th century. This courtyard inn was built for merchants from Bukhara — modern Uzbekistan, two thousand kilometres east — who crossed deserts and mountains to sell here and buy here. If the Silk Road had motorway service stations, this was the five-star one.

Here is how a caravanserai worked, and it is cleverer than it looks. The heavy arched portal was the only entrance, and it could be barred at night. Camels and goods stayed in the ground-floor stables and storerooms; merchants slept in the small cells above, arranged around the open courtyard so everyone could see everyone else's business. It was a warehouse, a hotel, a bank, and a trading floor in one building, and the rent on those little cells funded half the neighbourhood.

Think about what passed through this yard. Silk and spices from the east, obviously. But Baku's own exports too: salt, saffron, and naphtha — the crude oil that seeped out of the Absheron ground and that fire-temples had already been burning for centuries. The merchants sleeping upstairs were trading in the stuff that would, four hundred years later, turn this whole city into an oil boomtown.

One more thing. Sniff. The building is a restaurant now, and on most evenings the courtyard smells of grilling kebabs and fresh bread. The Silk Road traders would recognise the menu faster than the architecture. Have tea here if you like — it is the oldest dining room on this tour by about five hundred years — and then we walk to the Friday mosque.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander the courtyard. It operates as a restaurant, so food and tea are at menu prices.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard generally accessible through the day and evening with the restaurant. If the portal is shut, admire the carved stonework from the lane.
stops.accessibility: One step through the portal, then a level courtyard. The upper cells are not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the portal's carved frame before you go in — the stone muqarnas carving over the door is the building's finest original detail, and everyone photographs the courtyard instead.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard, turn left and walk south-west through the lanes for about two hundred metres, downhill toward the minaret you can see over the rooftops. The Juma Mosque is ahead of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Interfase, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Juma Mosque
stops.narration:
This is the Juma — the Friday Mosque, the congregation's mosque, the one the whole Old City traditionally walked to at noon on Fridays. People have prayed on this spot since at least the 12th century, and the minaret is the proof: look at its inscription band. It is dated 1437, which makes it older than most of the palace we are about to visit.

The prayer hall you see now is younger — a handsome 1899 rebuilding paid for with oil-boom money, when Baku's new millionaires were competing to fund mosques, theatres, and schools with their gusher fortunes. That is the pattern of this city: every fortune, whether khan's or oil baron's, eventually turned into stone. Walk around the outside first and look at the carved window frames and the portal. Then step in if it is open.

Inside it is calm in the particular way of working mosques: dome, mihrab pointing to Mecca, carpets, quiet. It is not a museum and it does not perform for visitors, which is exactly its charm.

House rules, and they matter. Take your shoes off at the door. Dress modestly — shoulders and knees covered, and women should cover their hair; scarves are usually available at the entrance. Do not visit during the five daily prayers or around Friday noon, when the mosque belongs to worshippers. If the door is shut, that is prayer time. The lanes around here are full of tea houses. You know what to do.

One thought to carry out with you: khans prayed here, oil barons prayed here, Soviet citizens whispered here. Empires queued up to own this city, and the mosque outlasted all of them.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working mosque, not a ticketed site. Donations for upkeep are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Open daily outside the five prayer times. Closed to tourists during prayers and for the Friday midday congregation. Prayer times shift daily.
stops.accessibility: A step or two at the entrance. Shoes are removed inside, so the floor is carpeted and level.
stops.insiderTip: Find the 1437 inscription band on the minaret — Kufic-style carving, easy to miss from the courtyard. It is the oldest dated thing on this stop by four and a half centuries.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque and walk north-west uphill through the lanes for about two hundred and fifty metres, following the signs for the palace complex. The big ceremonial portal ahead is the Palace of the Shirvanshahs.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Palace of the Shirvanshahs
stops.narration:
You are standing in front of the headquarters of one of the longest-lived dynasties in the Islamic world. The Shirvanshahs ruled this corner of the Caucasus for something like eight hundred years, and in the 1400s — their golden century — they built this hilltop complex as their seat: palace, court, mosque, tombs, and bathhouse, all in the honey-coloured limestone of the Absheron peninsula.

Do not look for one big palace. It is an ensemble, and the ensemble is the point. Start at the main residence, then find the Divankhana — the little open rotunda pavilion standing by itself in its own courtyard. Nobody agrees what it was: royal court? Memorial? Tomb for someone important? The leading theory changes every generation, which makes it the most argued-over pavilion in Azerbaijan. Then the royal mausoleum with its carved portal, the palace mosque with its slender 1441 minaret, and the bathhouse half-buried in the ground the way bathhouses were, for the steam.

Now the fall, because every palace needs one. In 1501 the Safavids took Shirvan, the dynasty ended, and the complex spent centuries as whatever the current regime needed — soldiers, stores, offices. What saved it was the stone itself: Absheron limestone carves like butter and weathers like iron, so the portals and inscriptions survived every indignity.

Give it a full forty-five minutes. Read the portal carvings slowly — the muqarnas vaulting over the doorways drips stone like frozen honey. And find a quiet corner of the upper courtyard: the view over the Old City rooftops to the bay is the sultans' version of our Maiden Tower panorama, minus the crowds.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Site ticket around 10 ₼, roughly. Verify at the gate — prices and foreign-visitor rates change, and some pavilions occasionally close for restoration.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 10:00 to 18:00. Ticket office usually closes an hour early. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Mixed: courtyards are cobbled with steps between levels, and several pavilions have stairs. The main courtyard is manageable; the full circuit is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: The Divankhana rotunda photographs best in slanting afternoon light, when the carving throws deep shadows. And ask the attendants which pavilion is closed — there is almost always one, and it is never the one you expected.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the palace complex and walk about fifty metres to the small museum house beside it — the Museum of Miniature Books, our next stop, is right next door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Museum of Miniature Books
stops.narration:
This is the smallest big museum in the world, and I mean that as the highest compliment. The Museum of Miniature Books was founded in 2002 by Zarifa Salakhova, who spent decades collecting tiny books until her private obsession needed its own building. It now holds thousands of miniature books from dozens of countries — one of the largest collections of its kind anywhere.

How tiny is tiny? The rule is roughly palm-sized and under, but the famous ones go much further: books barely bigger than a postage stamp, volumes you need the provided magnifying glasses to read, a complete classic you could post with a first-class stamp. There are miniature Qurans, miniature Pushkins, miniature atlases, miniature fairy tales in miniature languages. Somebody, somewhere, decided the complete works needed to fit in a matchbox, and somebody else agreed.

It is also, gloriously, free — Salakhova's founding principle was that wonder should not have a ticket price. The whole visit takes twenty minutes unless you are the kind of person who reads every label, in which case budget an hour and apologise to no one.

My favourite detail: the collection keeps growing because authors and publishers send new miniatures from all over the world. It is a museum with fan mail. Browse the cases slowly, borrow a magnifier, and find the smallest book in the room. Then find one smaller. There is always one smaller.

And enjoy the contrast, because in five minutes we walk out of the medieval walls entirely — from the tiniest books in Baku to the biggest square.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, by the founder's principle. Verify opening days at the door — small museums keep small hours.
stops.openingHours: Typically open late morning to late afternoon, roughly 11:00 to 17:00, and usually closed one weekday (often Monday). Small museum, shifting hours — check before counting on it.
stops.accessibility: Small interior with tight display rooms; mostly level but cramped. The entrance has a step or two.
stops.insiderTip: Ask to use a magnifying glass and hunt the tiniest book in the building — then check the case labels for which country sent the newest arrival. The collection spans more than seventy countries.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the museum and walk north-east through the lanes for about four hundred metres toward the old walls. Exit the Old City through the great double gate in the fortifications — the Shamakhi Gate, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Stanislav Kozlovskiy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Shamakhi Gate (Gosha Gala)
stops.narration:
Walk through this arch and you are walking through eight hundred years of border control. The Shamakhi Gate — the Gosha Gala, the Double Gates — is the great northern entrance of Icherisheher's medieval walls, and the road through it once led to Shamakhi, the old inland capital. Every invader, caravan, and oil baron you have met today came through a gate like this one.

Look at the masonry before you pass under. These fortifications went up in essentially their current form in the 12th century, when the Shirvanshahs moved their seat to Baku and decided their new capital needed proper walls. They are doubled in places — an inner and an outer line — which is what earns the name: gosha means paired, and the gates came in pairs too, so attackers who forced the first found themselves trapped in front of the second. Medieval security engineering, and it worked for centuries.

Touch the stone. Absheron limestone starts almost white and weathers to honey, and these blocks have been through Arabs, Persians, Russians, Soviets, and one very determined oil boom. The walls were inscribed with the Maiden Tower and the palace as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2000 — one listing, three monuments, all of which you have now visited.

Now turn around for the photo: the twin towers framing the Old City lanes behind you, with laundry and satellite dishes doing their best to photobomb eight centuries. Then walk out, because on the other side of this arch the medieval city ends and the 19th century begins — Fountain Square is two hundred metres ahead, and you will hear it before you see it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open fortifications, no ticket. It is a passage, not a site — walk through freely.
stops.accessibility: Level passage through the arch. The surrounding pavements are uneven in places.
stops.insiderTip: Photograph the gate from outside looking back in: the twin towers frame the Old City lanes perfectly, and late afternoon light hits the stone face-on.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north out of the gate for about two hundred metres toward the sound of water and café chatter. Fountain Square opens up in front of you — head for the fountains in the middle.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Самый древний, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Fountain Square
stops.narration:
And breathe out. You have just stepped from the 12th century into Baku's living room. Fountain Square is where the city comes to stroll, flirt, argue about football, and eat ice cream within splashing distance of a dozen fountains — and on a warm evening it holds more people than some villages.

It was not always fountains. In the 1800s this was a dusty parade square locals called the Parapet; the Soviets redesigned it with the fountains and the plane trees, and independent Azerbaijan filled the edges with boutiques and cafés. Look at the grand facade on one side — the Nizami Museum of Azerbaijani Literature, fronted by bronze statues of the country's great poets, Nizami chief among them. Baku has always believed poets deserve prime real estate.

Do what the locals do. Buy a tea or an ice cream, pick a bench, and watch: the backgammon games that get extremely competitive, the wedding parties doing photo circuits, the pigeons running a protection racket on the crumbs. This is also your last easy bathroom-and-snack stop before the hill, so use it.

Two errands before we move. First, check the time — you want to be on the hilltop for the golden hour, so linger here but not forever. Second, look south: the wooded hill rising over the rooftops is where we are going. There is a little railway that climbs it, built by the Soviets in 1960, with two tiny cars and enormous windows. It is called the funicular, it costs about a manat, and it is the most fun you can have in Baku for small change.

Finish your tea. We ride next.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free square. Cafés are at normal Baku prices. The funicular ride up next costs about 1 ₼ each way — carry coins or small notes.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Liveliest from late afternoon into the night.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free throughout. Benches everywhere.
stops.insiderTip: The Literature Museum facade statues read like a hall of fame of Azerbaijani poetry — find Nizami, the 12th-century epic poet the museum is named for. Evening, when the fountains are lit, is the square at its best.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south from the square for about fifteen minutes, downhill through the streets toward the bay, to the funicular lower station. Buy a ticket (about 1 ₼) and ride the little car to the top. If the funicular is closed for maintenance, take a taxi to Highland Park instead — do not attempt the steep road on foot in the heat.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Highland Park Viewpoint
stops.narration:
Was the funicular worth it? Turn around and answer. Below you the bay curves in a perfect U — the reason Baku exists, a natural harbour on a coast with few good ones — with the Old City's walls, the Maiden Tower, and three hundred metres of minarets packed along the water. Behind you the Flame Towers rise like three tongues of glass fire, flickering with LED flames after dark. This terrace, Dağüstü Park, is the best view in Azerbaijan, and you earned it with a one-manat train ticket.

Get your bearings. That rolled-carpet-shaped building on the waterfront is the Carpet Museum — yes, it is shaped like a rolled carpet, and yes, architects really did that. The long white hall further along the bay hosted Eurovision in 2012, the year Azerbaijan threw a party for the whole continent. The tankers and ferries threading the horizon are working the Caspian's oil and freight lanes, same as a century ago.

Now the wind. Remember the City of Winds? This is where you meet it personally. The khazri can gust hard enough to lean on up here, which is why your photo will have excellent hair. Hold onto hats, scarves, and small children.

Stay until the light goes golden — the limestone city turns honey-coloured and the bay goes silver, and for about twenty minutes every view is the good one. Then we walk the ridge south, because a hundred metres away this panorama shares a hilltop with the most solemn ground in the country, and the contrast is the whole point of Baku.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free viewpoint. The funicular up costs about 1 ₼ each way; verify it is running before walking to the lower station.
stops.openingHours: Terrace open access at all times. The funicular typically runs roughly 10:00 to late evening but closes for maintenance spells — check locally.
stops.accessibility: The funicular cars and the main terrace are step-manageable, but the park paths slope and gusty wind can unbalance. Take it slow on the ridge path.
stops.insiderTip: The twenty minutes before sunset are magic: the Old City glows honey-gold and the bay turns silver. After dark, stay a few minutes more — the Flame Towers' LED show starts and the boulevard lights string the whole bay.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south along the ridge path for about two hundred metres, past the Flame Towers, to the rows of glowing graves around the eternal flame. That is Martyrs' Alley — please go quietly.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Martyrs' Alley
stops.narration:
Lower your voice. This ground is sacred, and the tour changes tone here on purpose. Martyrs' Alley — Şəhidlər Xiyabanı — is where Azerbaijan buries those who died for its independence, row after row of graves with portrait photographs, red carnations, and dates that are far too recent.

Most of the graves are from Black January, 1990. As the Soviet Union was cracking, Moscow sent tanks into Baku on the night of the 19th of January to crush the independence movement. Around one hundred and thirty civilians died — shot, crushed, bayoneted. The funerals a few days later drew over a million mourners, and the victims were buried here on what had been a Soviet park. Within two years the empire that killed them no longer existed. The alley also holds martyrs of the Karabakh wars, and the dates on the stones keep going.

At the end of the avenue burns the eternal flame, lit in 1998 and never out since. Stand at it a moment. Then find the octagonal Turkish memorial nearby: it honours the Ottoman soldiers of the Caucasian Islamic Army who died retaking Baku in 1918. Two countries' griefs, one hilltop.

A confession about this place: in Soviet times this hill held a giant statue of a Bolshevik leader and a pleasure park. The city replaced all of that with graves and a flame. That tells you more about modern Azerbaijan than any museum label.

Etiquette, and it is non-negotiable: quiet voices, no picnics, no posed grinning selfies by the graves. Pay respects, walk the avenue slowly, and take the stairs down the east side when you are ready — the Caspian is waiting, and the living city does its celebrating down there.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free memorial, open to all. It is a place of mourning — treat it as one.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Visit in daylight or early evening; the flame burns through the night.
stops.accessibility: Level avenue along the ridge, step-free in the main memorial area. The descent stairs to the boulevard have many steps — take the path slowly.
stops.insiderTip: Read a few of the portrait plaques as you walk — ages, professions, families. The stones stop being a monument and start being neighbours. Then look up: the eternal flame with the bay behind it is the shot.
stops.nextStopDirections: Take the stairs and paths down the east side of the hill toward the water for about ten minutes, emerging on the seafront promenade by the rolled-carpet building. That is the Carpet Museum end of Baku Boulevard — our final stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: shankar s., CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Baku Boulevard
stops.narration:
You made it. Toes nearly in the Caspian. This promenade — Dənizkənarı, the Seaside National Park — is where Baku exhales, and after a day of towers, tombs, and tiny books, you have earned a bench with a sea view.

The boulevard started in 1909, when oil millionaires decided their boomtown needed a respectable waterfront and hired gardeners to plant one on the dusty shore. It worked so well that every generation since has extended it — what began as a short promenade now runs for kilometres in both directions, with gardens, fountains, rides, and the famous Little Venice canals a little further along.

Now look at the water, because it is lying to you. The Caspian looks like a sea, smells faintly like a sea, and has oil rigs and sturgeon like a sea — but it is a lake, the largest lake on earth, with a surface sitting some twenty-eight metres below ocean level. No tides to speak of, no outlet, and water levels that rise and fall over the decades like slow breathing. The beluga sturgeon down there produce the caviar that once bankrolled half this city's mansions.

Behind you is the Carpet Museum in its rolled-carpet building — worth a visit another day for the knotted dragons alone. Above you the Flame Towers are switching on. Ahead of you, ferries and the last of the sunset.

End-of-walk ritual, and I insist: buy tea from a promenade vendor, sit facing the water, and do nothing for ten minutes. You walked from a 12th-century tower to a lake that pretends to be a sea, through eight hundred years, for under three kilometres of actual walking. The wind is still blowing. It is always blowing. That is Baku telling you to come back.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free promenade. Vendors, cafés, boat rides and the museums along it charge separately.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best at sunset and into the evening; the promenade stays lively late.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, paved promenade — the most accessible stop on the tour. Benches throughout.
stops.insiderTip: Walk five minutes further along to Little Venice for the canals and bridges, and look back at the Flame Towers after full dark — the LED flame show is the city's goodnight.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stroll either direction along the promenade — cafés, tea vendors, and taxis line the boulevard. The city centre and Fountain Square are a short taxi or a twenty-minute stroll back north.
